title: Report on Crimes Against Humanity Committed by Hong Kong Government Officials in Hong Kong and Several Other Places
subtitle: FACTUAL SUMMARY

blocks.text: This report documents information providing a reasonable basis to believe that, since 2019 – and with substantial institutional expansion following the enactment of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region ("HKNSL") on 30 June 2020 – the authorities of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region ("HKSAR") and the People's Republic of China have carried out a widespread or systematic attack directed against an identifiable civilian population on political grounds within the meaning of Article 7 of the Rome Statute and customary international criminal law.
blocks.html: This report documents information providing a reasonable basis to believe that, since 2019 – and with substantial institutional expansion following the enactment of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region ("HKNSL") on 30 June 2020 – the authorities of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region ("HKSAR") and the People's Republic of China have carried out a widespread or systematic attack directed against an identifiable civilian population on political grounds within the meaning of Article 7 of the Rome Statute and customary international criminal law.

blocks.text: The civilian population targeted consists principally of participants in and supporters of the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement and, more broadly, persons identified by the authorities through actual or perceived political opinion, expression, association, journalism, civil-society activity, political participation or opposition to the prevailing political order. The affected population includes protesters, opposition politicians, journalists, editors, trade unionists, civil-society organisers, students, children, religious figures, human-rights defenders and members of the exiled Hong Kong pro-democracy community.

blocks.text: The principal crimes alleged are imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty in violation of fundamental rules of international law under Article 7(1)(e), and persecution on political grounds under Article 7(1)(h). The evidence concerning custodial beatings, prolonged solitary confinement, sexual violence and other serious mistreatment provides additional support for allegations under Articles 7(1)(f), 7(1)(g) and 7(1)(k).

blocks.text: The alleged attack has been implemented through an integrated State apparatus rather than through isolated acts of individual misconduct. Relevant institutions include the Hong Kong Police Force and its National Security Department, the Department of Justice, specialised national-security bodies, designated national-security judges, the Correctional Services Department, the Security Bureau, the Committee for Safeguarding National Security and other executive and administrative institutions. The system operates through legislation, arrest and investigative powers, restrictive bail provisions, prosecution, adjudication, imprisonment, correctional measures and continuing restrictions after release.

blocks.text: The scale and duration of the conduct support its widespread character. More than 10,000 persons were arrested in connection with the 2019 protests and related political activity. Approximately 2,200 persons have been sent to prison on politically related charges since 2019. During the first six months of the 2019 protests, the authorities acknowledged approximately 16,000 discharges of tear gas, approximately 13,900 rounds of ammunition of various types, and approximately 2,600 persons seeking emergency medical treatment in public hospitals in connection with protest-related events. Children were among those arrested and subjected to custodial and national-security measures.

blocks.text: The systematic character of the attack is demonstrated by the repeated use of substantially similar measures against different sectors of civilian society over a period of years. Opposition politicians were imprisoned for organising and participating in an electoral primary; journalists and editors were prosecuted for political publications; the leaders of the organisation that for three decades organised the commemoration of those killed in the Tiananmen Square massacre on 4 June 1989 were sentenced to up to seven years and three months' imprisonment for incitement to subversion; professionals were imprisoned for allegorical children's books; students were prosecuted for low-reach political expression; and elderly or seriously ill activists were imprisoned for planned symbolic protest. These cases demonstrate a recurring pattern directed at political expression and participation rather than a narrow campaign against violent conduct.

blocks.text: The deprivation of liberty has been reinforced by a differentiated national-security procedural regime. Relevant measures include the reverse presumption against bail under Article 42(2) of the HKNSL, prolonged pre-trial detention, extended detention powers, restrictions upon access to chosen legal representatives, removal of trial by jury in specified national-security cases, adjudication by judges designated under the national-security framework, compulsory information-gathering powers and binding executive certificates on specified national-security questions.

blocks.text: Independent international findings substantially reinforce the allegation of arbitrary political detention. The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has found the detention of prominent Hong Kong political defendants, including Chow Hang-tung, Jimmy Lai and Owen Chow Ka-shing, to be arbitrary. United Nations mechanisms have additionally raised concerns regarding prolonged solitary confinement, judicial independence, the reverse bail regime and allegations that evidence used in national-security proceedings was obtained through torture. The continued maintenance and expansion of the same system after repeated international notice supports the inference that its operation reflects State policy rather than inadvertence, institutional error or isolated misconduct.

blocks.text: The alleged attack also encompasses the response of State institutions to violence against the targeted political population. The events at Yuen Long on 21 July 2019 are particularly significant. The evidence includes public statements preceding the attack calling for action against protesters, advance warnings received by police, prolonged non-intervention while organised groups assaulted civilians, subsequent official characterisation of the violence as a clash, selective enforcement affecting persons associated with the protest movement, and the rejection of demands for an independent inquiry. Taken cumulatively, these circumstances support an inference of State acquiescence rather than an isolated or accidental failure of police response. (See EXHIBITS C6–C11)

The overseas programme includes arrest warrants, public monetary bounties, statutory "specified absconder" measures, financial and professional restrictions, threats against persons providing support, reprisals against family members, and organised surveillance and intelligence-gathering abroad.

blocks.text: Senior officials expressly acknowledged and endorsed the international reach of that programme. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu stated that wanted political opponents would be pursued "for life", would live "in fear every day", and that Hong Kong's national-security legislation possessed "the same power of taking extraterritorial action against criminals" as the laws of other States. Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung stated that the authorities would identify the contacts, associates and financiers of wanted persons "in Hong Kong or overseas" and repeatedly threatened continuing pursuit and isolation of those targeted. (See EXHIBITS F5–F16)

blocks.text: The bounty programme itself solicited information concerning the movements and circumstances of named dissidents residing abroad and invited persons "in Hong Kong or overseas" to provide such intelligence. It thereby created a direct incentive to locate, monitor and report upon political opponents residing in foreign States. The authorities also expressly referred to persons who had "sought protection from foreign countries", while the programme provided means of continuing their pursuit notwithstanding the practical limits of ordinary inter-State legal cooperation. (See EXHIBITS F8 & F17)

blocks.text: The clearest territorial nexus under Article 12(2)(a) concerns the United Kingdom, a State Party to the Rome Statute. Criminal proceedings, official records and judicial findings establish that surveillance, operational tasking, acquisition and transmission of personal information, misuse of United Kingdom government systems, deception and other operational activity were physically carried out in the United Kingdom against persons associated with the exiled Hong Kong pro-democracy community. Payments connected with such operations were made through the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London. Following a contested trial, two participants were convicted, and United Kingdom authorities identified the relevant foreign intelligence service as the Hong Kong Police Force and described the activities as a "shadow policing operation" and transnational repression. (See EXHIBITS F28–F37)

Separately, Article 12(2)(b) may provide jurisdiction over particular alleged perpetrators who are established to be nationals of the United Kingdom, Portugal or another State Party.

blocks.text: Complementarity does not presently bar further examination of the principal potential cases identified in this report. The United Kingdom has genuinely prosecuted operational actors Chung Biu (Bill) Yuen and Chi Leung (Peter) Wai for conduct carried out within the United Kingdom, but those proceedings concerned different accused persons from the senior Hong Kong officials identified here. Likewise, the prosecution in Hong Kong of persons alleged to be victims of political persecution does not constitute investigation or prosecution of the officials alleged to have designed, directed, implemented or contributed to that persecution. No domestic proceeding identified in the present record investigates or prosecutes John Lee Ka-chiu or Chris Tang Ping-keung for substantially the same conduct forming the basis of the potential cases described in this report. The detailed Article 17 analysis is set out in Part 13.

Imprisonment and persecution are themselves expressly enumerated crimes that were committed within the contextual attack required by Article 7.

sections.title: Jurisdiction Based on Nationality – Article 12(2)(b)

blocks.text: Article 12(2)(b) of the Rome Statute provides that the ICC may exercise jurisdiction where the person accused of a crime within the jurisdiction of the ICC is a national of a State Party. The United Kingdom and Portugal are States Parties to the Rome Statute.

blocks.text: British National (Overseas) [BN(O)] is a form of British nationality recognised under United Kingdom law. Section 67(1) of the International Criminal Court Act 2001 (U.K.) expressly includes a British National (Overseas), together with a British citizen and certain other categories of British nationality, within the statutory definition of a "United Kingdom national" for the purposes of Part 5 of that Act. (See EXHIBITS A1 & A2)

sections.title: Territorial Jurisdiction – Article 12(2)(a)

blocks.text: A separate and independent jurisdictional basis arises under Article 12(2)(a) from conduct occurring on the territory of States Parties.

blocks.text: The principal policy alleged in this report was formulated and implemented substantially in Hong Kong, which is not itself territory of a State Party to the Rome Statute. The alleged course of conduct, however, has not remained wholly within Hong Kong. Since at least 2023, components of the alleged programme of persecution against the exiled Hong Kong pro-democracy community have been carried out within the territory of States Parties, most concretely within the United Kingdom.

blocks.title: Article 7(1)(e) – Imprisonment or other severe deprivation of physical liberty in violation of fundamental rules of international law

blocks.text:
The conduct relevant to Article 7(1)(e) includes:
The mass arrest, detention and imprisonment of protesters, political activists, former legislators, journalists and others in connection with the exercise of freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, association and political participation.
The application of national-security offences to peaceful political and expressive conduct that international human-rights bodies and organisations have identified as conduct that should not have been criminalised.
An analysis of national-security cases contained in EXHIBIT C34 found that bail was denied in approximately 89 per cent of the cases examined, with an average period of pre-trial detention of approximately 11 months. This pattern, operating under the reverse presumption contained in Article 42 of the HKNSL, has resulted in prolonged pre-trial imprisonment of political defendants, in some cases extending for years before trial. (See EXHIBIT C34)
The detention of persons whose deprivation of liberty has subsequently been determined by the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention to be arbitrary and incompatible with fundamental international human-rights standards. (See EXHIBITS B4, B5 & B10)
The use of Care and Protection Orders under the Protection of Children and Juveniles Ordinance (Cap. 213) against minors who had not been charged with criminal offences, including the detention of a 13-year-old for 27 days with restrictions upon contact with her family before a magistrate rejected the application. (See EXHIBIT C35)

blocks.title: Article 7(1)(h) – Persecution against an identifiable group on political grounds

blocks.text:
The information described throughout this report is also relevant to persecution under Article 7(1)(h), through the intentional and severe deprivation of fundamental rights of persons identified by reason of political opinion or political activity, in connection with other acts described in Article 7(1), particularly imprisonment and severe deprivation of physical liberty.
The conduct relied upon includes:
the sustained use of criminal proceedings, detention and imprisonment against persons identified through their participation in or support for the pro-democracy movement.
the dismantling of political opposition, independent media organisations, trade unions and civil-society organisations through criminal proceedings and national-security enforcement directed at their political activities.
the imprisonment of persons for peaceful expression, publication, journalism, political slogans, peaceful political organisation and other non-violent forms of participation.
the direction of criminal proceedings against conduct protected by the rights to freedom of expression, assembly, association and political participation. An analysis of concluded national-security cases found that approximately 85 per cent involved only the legitimate exercise of freedom of expression that should not have been criminalised. (See EXHIBIT C34)
the systematic use of national-security procedural restrictions against political defendants, including the reverse presumption against bail, removal of trial by jury, restrictions upon access to counsel of one's choosing, and the assignment of specially designated national-security judges.
the continued threat of prosecution against approximately 7,000 persons arrested in connection with the 2019 protests but not charged, whose cases have reportedly remained open for years and have been linked to "rehabilitation", "re-education" or political-assimilation measures. (See EXHIBIT C35)
the programme of transnational repression against exiled members of the same political population, including arrest warrants, public monetary bounties, "specified absconder" measures, surveillance and intelligence-gathering, restrictions upon financial support, and reprisals against family members, as described in Part 10.

sections.title: Structural failure of the police complaints system

blocks.text: The principal statutory body responsible for monitoring complaints against police is the Independent Police Complaints Council ("IPCC").
blocks.html: The principal statutory body responsible for monitoring complaints against police is the Independent Police Complaints Council ("IPCC").

blocks.text: The IPCC does not itself conduct the initial investigation of complaints. sections.title: The Yuen Long attack and State acquiescence

blocks.text: The attack at Yuen Long on 21 July 2019 is particularly relevant to the relationship between political violence, official conduct and the treatment of perceived opponents during the protest period.

blocks.text: On the evening of 21 July 2019, organised groups of armed men attacked civilians at and around Yuen Long MTR station. The persons assaulted included protesters, journalists, local residents and passengers with no apparent involvement in the demonstrations. (See EXHIBIT C6)

blocks.text: Police also received repeated emergency calls and advance warnings concerning the developing violence but did not intervene for an extended period, allowing the attacks to continue. (See EXHIBITS C8 & C9)

blocks.text: The response after the attack reinforced the significance of the failure to intervene.

blocks.text: Police publicly characterised the events as a clash despite extensive video evidence showing groups of armed men attacking civilians. Subsequent enforcement was selective: persons who had been attacked or who had confronted the assailants were themselves arrested or imprisoned, while accountability for many of those involved in the original violence was substantially delayed. (See EXHIBITS C10 & C11)

blocks.text: The evidence concerning Yuen Long must therefore be considered cumulatively: official statements preceding the violence; advance warnings received by police; prolonged non-intervention during the attacks; subsequent official characterisation of the events; selective enforcement against persons associated with the protest movement; and the failure to establish an independent mechanism capable of examining the police command decisions surrounding the incident.

blocks.text: Taken cumulatively, the evidence supports an inference of State acquiescence rather than an isolated or accidental failure of police response. Public statements preceding the violence called for action against protesters in Yuen Long; police received advance warnings and repeated emergency calls; intervention was substantially delayed while organised violence continued; police subsequently reframed the attacks as a clash; enforcement was directed in part against persons who had been attacked or had confronted the assailants; and demands for an independent investigation into the police response were rejected. (See EXHIBITS C7–C11)

blocks.text: The significance of Yuen Long therefore lies not merely in police non-intervention on a single evening, but in the cumulative relationship between prior official encouragement, advance notice, prolonged non-intervention, subsequent official characterisation, selective enforcement and the absence of an independent inquiry. These circumstances form part of the broader evidence that violence against persons identified with the protest movement was tolerated and subsequently treated differently from conduct attributed to the political opposition.

sections.title: Cumulative significance

blocks.text: The evidence in this Part demonstrates that political imprisonment in Hong Kong cannot be assessed solely by counting convictions and formal sentences.

parts.title: Extraterritorial Conduct in the Territory of States Parties to the Rome Statute

blocks.text: The course of conduct described in this report has not been confined to the territory of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

blocks.text: Since 2023, the Hong Kong authorities have pursued a coordinated programme directed against members of the exiled Hong Kong pro-democracy community, including persons known by the authorities to reside in States Parties to the Rome Statute, particularly the United Kingdom, as well as Canada, Germany and Australia.
blocks.html: Since 2023, the Hong Kong authorities have pursued a coordinated programme directed against members of the exiled Hong Kong pro-democracy community, including persons known by the authorities to reside in States Parties to the Rome Statute, particularly the United Kingdom, as well as Canada, Germany and Australia.

blocks.text: The programme has included four interrelated forms of conduct: first, arrest warrants and public monetary bounties against named persons residing overseas; secondly, statutory "specified absconder" measures imposing financial and civil disabilities upon named persons and threatening criminal liability against those who support them; thirdly, coercive measures against family members remaining in Hong Kong; and fourthly, operational surveillance and intelligence-gathering carried out within the United Kingdom through persons associated with the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in London.

parts.title: Relevant International Criminal Law Precedents and Contemporary ICC Practice

blocks.text: The conduct described in this report does not require the creation of a novel category of crime against humanity.

International criminal jurisprudence has repeatedly recognised that crimes against humanity may be committed through imprisonment, persecution, discriminatory legal systems, detention institutions and the organised use of State or quasi-State power against civilian populations.

children.html: The most relevant authorities concern five issues central to this report:

items.html: territorial jurisdiction over transboundary crimes;
imprisonment and severe deprivation of liberty;
persecution through deprivation of fundamental rights;
the use of legal, judicial and detention institutions as instruments of an attack; and
the fact that conduct presented domestically as law enforcement remains capable of constituting crimes against humanity.

These functions correspond to the institutional pattern described throughout this report:

items.html: police and security agencies identify, investigate and arrest targeted persons;
prosecutors invoke national-security and sedition legislation against political activity;
statutory provisions impose differentiated bail, detention and procedural rules;
designated courts adjudicate the resulting prosecutions;
correctional institutions implement imprisonment and additional restrictions;
executive authorities maintain, defend and expand the system; and
the same security apparatus pursues members of the targeted political population after they leave Hong Kong.
